title: Joint symmetry and dynamical accessibility in compact Hamiltonian encodings of set cover
abstract: Which part of a Hamiltonian spectrum is physically relevant when both the initial state and interpolation preserve several symmetries? We address this question for a compact multi-register encoding of Minimum Set Cover. The represented symmetry combines register permutations with the faithful base action of the incidence automorphism group. We distinguish its fixed, symmetry-allowed space from the generally smaller cyclic space generated by the protocol and define gaps relative to isolated bands in that space. A sector-resolved Schur-complement bound certifies cover-measurement probability whenever the sector contains feasible covers and has positive invalid-state separation; the sector kinetic floor is essential. Exact orbit quotients expose inter-sector coincidences invisible to a symmetric protocol, while a stability theorem shows that transverse dark crossings persist under small symmetry-preserving perturbations. On an even-cycle family, the original linear interpolation has an exact global multiplicity closure while the joint-fixed excitation gap remains constant. For the same family we construct a Johnson/Metropolis parent path from a Dicke state to a Gibbs-amplitude state with cover probability $1-O(n^{-5})$. A zero-range comparison and a log-concave three-box coupling give the uniform cyclic-gap certificate $Ω(n^{-13})$. Quantitative derivative bounds then yield a polynomial adiabatic runtime in the abstract Hamiltonian-access model, conditional on Dicke-state preparation and access to the parent Hamiltonian. We make no quantum-speedup claim: the result is a rigorous separation of global, symmetry-allowed, and dynamically accessible spectral structure. Changing the initial state or breaking a preserved symmetry changes that accessible spectrum.
summary: This theoretical paper analyzes the spectral properties of quantum Hamiltonians used to encode NP-hard problems like Set Cover. It rigorously distinguishes between the full symmetry-allowed spectrum and the subspace actually reachable by the system's dynamics. The work provides structural guarantees regarding adiabatic evolution times, establishing a fundamental separation between potential symmetries and actual physical accessibility.
main_problem: The research addresses which parts of a Hamiltonian spectrum are physically relevant when both the initial state preparation and subsequent time evolution preserve multiple symmetries, specifically for encoding Minimum Set Cover.
main_result: The authors establish a rigorous structural separation between the global symmetry-allowed spectral structure and the dynamically accessible cyclic subspace. They derive bounds on the adiabatic runtime conditional on specific state preparations.
method: The analysis employs advanced mathematical tools including sector-resolved localization, analyzing algebraic structures generated by Hamiltonians, and deriving gap estimates using techniques related to Dirichlet forms and coupling arguments.
model_or_system: The model is a compact multi-register quantum encoding of the Minimum Set Cover problem. The dynamics are governed by complex Hamiltonians involving walk terms, cover constraints, and exclusion terms acting on multiple registers.
key_observables: Joint fixed excitation gap, sector-resolved leakage bounds ($\Gamma_\gamma$), and the dynamically accessible cyclic space ($\mathcal{K}_u$).
important_parameters: The size of the problem instance ($n$), the number of registers, and parameters governing the Hamiltonian components ($\lambda, \mu$).
main_assumptions: No quantum speedup claim is made; the results are structural separations. The analysis relies on specific conditions for symmetry sectors and state preparation (e.g., Dicke-state preparation).
paper_structure: The paper progresses by defining the physical system and Hamiltonian, establishing the relationship between different spectral subspaces ($H_{	ext{sym}}$ vs $\mathcal{K}_u$), proving localization bounds (Proposition 1), constructing explicit parent paths for specific families, and finally deriving polynomial adiabatic runtime estimates.
why_interesting: The rigorous separation of accessible spectral structure is highly relevant to understanding the limitations and guarantees of quantum computation protocols based on Hamiltonian simulation or annealing.
